Adult females of the Longjawed Orbweaver (Tetragnatha versicolor) attain a cephalothorax length of 1.33 cm [Li = 1.33 cm], a measurement that places them among the larger members of their genus. This ultimate size reflects the considerable investment in somatic growth required before resources can be channeled into reproduction. Males, in contrast, are notably smaller, reaching a final cephalothorax length of only 0.92 cm [Li = 0.92 cm], a pronounced sexual dimorphism that is common among orb-weaving spiders and is often linked to the males' more active searching strategy for mates. The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult is recorded at 0.082 g [Wwi = 0.082 g], a mass that correlates strongly with the female's capacity to produce large egg clutches. Field surveys typically capture these dimensions from mature individuals during the peak of the breeding season, providing reliable reference points for the species' maximum body size.

This wet weight at puberty is a critical life-history milestone, signaling the transition from the sub-adult, pre-reproductive phase to the reproductively active adult phase. This suggests a univoltine life cycle in many temperate populations, with individuals completing their entire existence within a single year, a pattern observed in numerous small-bodied arthropods.

Reproductive output in the Longjawed Orbweaver is impressive, particularly when females receive abundant nutrition.
